chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
title: Tommy Dorsey's taste for showmanship: Shavers and Lunceford
summary: Freeman says Dorsey valued showy jazz like Charlie Shavers and the commercial Lunceford band, not pure players like Buck Clayton.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Was Sy Oliver in that band?
No, Sy came along much later than that. You see, Tommy always admired the Lunceford band.

The one thing that Tommy loved in a man's playing -- just playing jazz was not important enough -- that jazz had to have showmanship in it. Therefore -- well, a perfect reason for saying that is that he absolutely idolized Charles Shavers, and Charlie Shavers was a brilliant player but he was a theatrical player -- everything was done for an effect although he was a highly talented guy and I loved him, you know, but Tommy thought that Charlie Shavers was the greatest thing that ever happened, because Charlie Shavers would make up all kinds of contrived little phrases in a given theme.

Like, he would play other songs in a theme, anything to be tricky and clever, you see, and Tommy ate that up. Tommy didn't see through that as being kind of synthetic jazz, but Charlie Shavers was a great trumpet player. Don't understand, nor do I want anybody who hears
this or reads this, Charlie Shavers was a very talented guy. But that was the way he played and Tommy thought it was great.
I don't think Tommy would be a great admirer of a guy like Buck Clayton, who was a pure player.
I mean the point is it comes out in taste, and if you got that kind of taste, you got it. It's not what you call good taste in music. It may be good taste as far as selling a product is concerned.

And so the Lunceford band, although it was a super band, was a pretty commercial band. The guys with the horns up in the air, all done beautifully, and very swingingly, but that was what Tommy's idea of a great jazz band, you see.
And so he loved Sy Oliver's arrangements, thought Sy Oliver was a genius.

Oh, Well, Sy Oliver is a highly talented man from way back. But I was speaking specifically of the style of the Lunceford band. I don't think it was built [unintelligible] around Sy -- one of the powerful writers.
But Tommy loved the musicality of the band also and that would be Sy Oliver's -- so when he got a chance to get Sy, he grabbed on fast, and I think Sy -- of course, Sy is a big success today.

Well, Sy is operating on the same principle today. Sy is selling a nice musical product. He plays waltzes, he plays rhumbas or what have you, Latin American things, and he's very smooth and he's very nice and it's musical. It's very nice but, of course, it's a musical product.
